y-m-65-07.thinking.0: Decide whether you can tell objects apart

y-m-65-03.prereq.0: H2/H3 label for dis task na only difficulty level assigned for production. E no mean curriculum assign subject to dat grade.
y-m-65-03.title: Two people for class fit get same birthday?
y-m-65-03.topic: Complement events and probability multiplication: chance say at least one pair match
y-m-65-03.goal: Explain why the probability of 'at least one' is found from the opposite case instead of counting directly, and decide how the probability changes when assumptions change.
y-m-65-03.material: In a class of 30 students, find whether at least 2 share a birthday. Model: each student's birthday is one of 365 days, every day is equally likely, and students do not affect each other. Ignore leap years.
y-m-65-03.prereq.1: Multiply the probabilities of independent events
y-m-65-03.prereq.3: Condition: a birthday is one of 365 days (no February 29), every day is equally likely, and students' birthdays are assumed independent.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.prompt: Let's think step by step about the probability that at least one pair of students shares a birthday.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write one line saying what information your prediction was based on.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether new information strong enough to change your guess or whether e fit remain same.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.info: In a class of 30, how likely do you think at least one pair shares a birthday? You have not calculated yet.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which one near your intuition pass?
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Right now, either answer is just intuition. The important point is that 30 people make 435 pairs.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: It assumed 365 days is far more than 30 people, so overlaps are rare.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: It assumed overlaps happen once in a while.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It took into account that the number of pairs is large.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.info: These are probabilities for small groups: 5 people, about 2.7%; 10 people, about 11.7%; 20 people, about 41.1%; 23 people, about 50.7%.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Wetin be your guess for 30 people now?
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.after: The probability grows as the number of people grows, and it already passes 50% at 23 people, so for 30 it is higher.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It assumed the increase grows in a straight line as people are added.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It continued the upward trend that passes 50% at 23 people.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It assumed the probability can decrease even as people are added.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.info:
The probability that all 30 people have different birthdays is (365/365)×(364/365)×...×(336/365), about 29.4%. So the chance of at least one matching pair is 1 minus this, about 70.6%.
Now think about real life. Students' birthdays are not spread evenly across seasons; they cluster in certain months.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: If birthdays are clustered, how does the probability of at least one matching pair compare with 70.6%?
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.after: Even spread gives the fewest overlaps. If birthdays cluster, the chance that the same day overlaps is the same or higher. So 70.6% is likely lower than the real value.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: It assumed that clustering makes birthdays avoid each other.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It assumed the calculation stays the same even if the model changes.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It does not become less than 70.6%.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: It assumed that clustering makes the same days overlap more often.
y-m-65-03.s.s1.reflect: Look back at how you changed your first intuition after the calculation and changed assumptions, or what information helped you keep it.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.prompt: Explain why you use 'all different' instead of counting the probability of 'at least one matching pair' directly.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.hint.0: If you list matching-pair cases directly, write a few different forms they can take.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the 'all different' case has only one form.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Your reason why direct counting hard specific?
y-m-65-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you connect subtracting from 1 to the fact that probabilities add up to 1?
y-m-65-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you consider whether the same method works for numbers of people other than 30?
y-m-65-03.s.s2.model.0: Matching-pair cases come in too many forms, like only one pair matching, two pairs matching, or three people matching, so they are hard to count directly. The opposite case, 'all different', has only one form, so multiplication finds it directly, and subtracting from 1 makes it easy.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.model.1: The total probability is 1, so find the probability that no pair matches and subtract it from 1. You only need the all-different case, so the calculation is much simpler.
y-m-65-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: It does not use the words 'complement event', but it is the same idea.

y-m-65-01.title: When 'choose two people' fit mean two different things
y-m-65-01.topic: Permutations and combinations: rule for treating chosen results as same
y-m-65-01.goal: Explain say even for same 'choose 2 out of 5', number of cases change when rule for distinguishing results different, and find line with double-counting mistake in solution.
y-m-65-01.material:
Dem choose two people from 5 candidates (가, 나, 다, 라, 마). Each person fit choose only once.
Situation ㄱ: Di two chosen people get different positions, class president and vice president.
Situation ㄴ: Di two chosen people together get same role, class representatives.
You wan compare number of cases in both situations.
y-m-65-01.thinking.0: Check rule for treating results as same
y-m-65-01.thinking.2: Make your own examples and explain rule for telling results apart
y-m-65-01.prereq.0: H2/H3 label for dis task na only difficulty level assigned for production. E no mean curriculum assign subject to dat grade.
y-m-65-01.prereq.1: Product rule for counting (count cases by multiplying)
y-m-65-01.prereq.2: Condition: all 5 candidates na different people, and nobody fit choose twice
y-m-65-01.s.s1.prompt: Wetin you think now about number of cases for situations ㄱ and ㄴ?
y-m-65-01.s.s1.hint.0: For ㄱ, write separately result '가 na president and 나 na vice president' and result '나 na president and 가 na vice president.'
y-m-65-01.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many ways same two people (가, 나) dey written as results for ㄴ.
y-m-65-01.s.s1.o.a: ㄱ get more. Na because if position change, dem count am as different result
y-m-65-01.s.s1.r.a: E pay attention to rule for distinguishing results (position).
y-m-65-01.s.s1.o.b: Number of cases same for both situations, since dem choose 2 people. Na because same number of people dem choose
y-m-65-01.s.s1.r.b: E only look number of people dem choose and no check rule for distinguishing results.
y-m-65-01.s.s1.o.c: ㄴ get more. Na because roles same, so dem fit choose more people
y-m-65-01.s.s1.r.c: E read roles being same as meaning say range of people to choose wider.
y-m-65-01.s.s1.explain: For ㄱ, (가 president, 나 vice president) and (나 president, 가 vice president) na different results; but for ㄴ dem na same two representatives, so na one result. ㄱ get 20 cases and ㄴ get 10.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.prompt: One student solve situation ㄴ like dis. Choose wrong line.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether each line talk how many times dem count each result.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write yourself how many times (가, 나) and (나, 가) each appear in this solution multiplication.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.0: Count ways to choose 2 representatives from 5 candidates.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.1: You get 5 choices for first person and remaining 4 for second, so treating first and second as different gives 5×4=20 ways.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.2: (가, 나) and (나, 가) are the same representatives, but multiplication above counts them only once.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.line.3: So number of cases in situation ㄴ is 20.
y-m-65-01.s.s2.explain: 5×4 counts with 'first' and 'second' separate, so it counts (가, 나) and (나, 가) separately. Line 3 says 'count only once', which is wrong, so 20 ways in line 4 is wrong too. Same representative pair was counted 2 times each, so answer is 10.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.prompt: Make one situation where order (role) must count as different and another where it need not, then write the rule for telling them apart in one sentence.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.hint.0: For each situation, first ask: 'If the two people switch places, does the result change?'
y-m-65-01.s.s3.hint.1: Think of a case where the chosen people get different jobs (for example, read a book, give a presentation) and another where they all do the same job.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether your examples show the difference between the two rules for telling results apart?
y-m-65-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you test yourself whether swapping positions changes the result?
y-m-65-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate the number of cases?
y-m-65-01.s.s3.model.0: Example where order matters: choose a presenter and a host from 5 people. If they switch roles, the result is different, so order matters. Example where order does not matter: choose 2 students from 5 for cleaning duty. They do the same job, so switching gives the same result.
y-m-65-01.s.s3.model.1: Choosing who gets 1st and 2nd place in a race is a case where a different order gives a different result. Choosing 2 people to run in the same group is a case where switching still gives the same group, so order does not matter.

y-m-65-02.title: Same 8 moves, different road shape
y-m-65-02.topic: Number of paths: same number of moves, different maps
y-m-65-02.goal: Understand that even with the same number of moves, the number of shortest paths changes depending on how many moves go right and up; make your own map meeting the condition.
y-m-65-02.material: To go from home to school, move right (→) a times and up (↑) b times, for a total of a+b=8 moves. Each map has different a and b. Move one square at a time, only right or up, and no road is blocked. Write a shortest path as a line of 8 symbols made of → and ↑.
y-m-65-02.thinking.1: Make several maps that meet di condition
y-m-65-02.prereq.1: Experience counting paths by arranging repeated things or using combinations
y-m-65-02.prereq.2: Condition: move one square at a time, only right or up; every intersection is passable (nothing is blocked)
y-m-65-02.s.s1.prompt: Between the map (a, b)=(4, 4) and map (2, 6), which do you think has more shortest paths?
y-m-65-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write a few lines arranging 2 → symbols and 6 ↑ symbols in 8 spaces.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how many ways you can first choose the spaces for → on the two maps.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.o.a: The (4, 4) map has more. The two directions are mixed evenly.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.r.a: It thought an even split between directions gives more varied routes.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.o.b: The (2, 6) map has more because more moves go up.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.r.b: It thought the direction with more moves increases the number of routes.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.o.c: The two maps are the same because the total number of moves is the same.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.r.c: It looked only at the total number of moves and did not consider how the directions are split.
y-m-65-02.s.s1.explain: For (4, 4), choose 4 of 8 spaces for →, giving 70 ways; for (2, 6), choose 2 spaces for →, giving 28 ways.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 maps (a, b) with different shapes, where a+b=8 and there are at least 50 shortest paths. (Treat swapped a and b as the same shape.)
y-m-65-02.s.s2.hint.0: Try a=0, 1, 2, ... one by one and compare the ways to choose spaces for →.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.hint.1: First find the path count for the maps with the smallest and largest values, then narrow down toward the middle.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b gats be integers no smaller than 0.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.ok.c3: This map get at least 50 shortest routes.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.fail.c3: This map no get 50 shortest routes.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.explain: (4, 4) has 70 ways; (3, 5) and (5, 3) have 56 ways. (2, 6) has 28 ways and (1, 7) has 8 ways, which are not enough.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain how you found the number of shortest paths for the map you chose.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: If you write a path as a line of → and ↑, think what you need to decide to fix the line.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether switching → and ↑ ever gives the same path.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: E clear why you turn path to 8 spaces?
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you account for the fact that swapping identical → symbols gives the same path?
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you calculate the actual number using the method you wrote?
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.model.0: This means choosing 3 of 8 spaces for →, so it is the number of ways to choose 3 from 8: 56 ways.
y-m-65-02.s.s2.because.model.1: This is arranging 3 → and 5 ↑ in a line, but swapping identical symbols keeps the path the same, so divide 8! by 3! and 5! to get 56.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.prompt: On the (4, 4) map, one intersection is closed for construction and cannot be passed. What must you know to find the number of shortest paths?
y-m-65-02.s.s3.hint.0: Think separately about paths blocked by the construction and paths not blocked.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.hint.1: Choose 2 intersections (e.g. beside the start and beside the destination), count routes passing through each, and compare whether they are similar.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.o.a: Knowing only the total number of shortest routes on the (4, 4) map is enough.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.r.a: You must subtract routes passing through the blocked place from the total, and that number depends on where the blocked place is.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.o.b: It is enough to know only whether the blocked intersection is closer to the start or the destination.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.r.b: With rough distance only, you no fit count how many paths pass through that meeting point.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.o.c: You need to know how many blocks the intersection is from home in the → direction and in the ↑ direction.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.r.c: To subtract routes passing through the blocked intersection, you need its exact location.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.o.d: No extra information is needed except that one place is blocked. The number of routes through any intersection is about the same.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.r.d: Number of paths through each meeting point fit differ plenty.
y-m-65-02.s.s3.explain: The number of paths removed depends on which intersection is blocked. For example, a crossing beside the start and one near the destination are passed by very different numbers of paths.

y-m-65-04.title: Ball wey you put aside without looking affect next ball?
y-m-65-04.topic: Conditional probability: probability change when you get information?
y-m-65-04.goal: Separate how the probability of the same event changes when you know information and when you do not, and build a bag setup that meets the condition yourself.
y-m-65-04.material: A bag has 6 white balls and 4 black balls. They are the same shape and well mixed. Take one ball out, put it aside without looking at its color, then take out another.
y-m-65-04.thinking.2: Build model wey fit di condition
y-m-65-04.prereq.1: Basic probability idea, multiplication rule, or meaning of conditional probability
y-m-65-04.prereq.2: Condition: every ball is equally likely to be picked, and a ball taken out is not put back.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.prompt: If you do not know the color of the ball put aside, what is the probability that the second ball is white?
y-m-65-04.s.s1.hint.0: To compare with 6/10, first list all possible colors of the removed ball and write the probability for each case.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.hint.1: Multiply the probability of each case and add them, then compare with the original 6/10.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.o.a: Less than 6/10. With one fewer ball, the proportion of white balls also decreases.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.r.a: It looked only at the reduced number of balls and did not consider that the color is unknown.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.o.b: Exactly 6/10. If you do not know the removed ball's color, the second draw is under the same conditions as the first.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.r.b: If the color is unknown, treat the first ball as drawn under the same conditions as the second.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.o.c: Greater than 6/10. The first ball is more likely to be white.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.r.c: It assumed the first ball was biased toward white. You must consider the black case too.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.o.d: 5/9. The remaining balls are 5 white and 4 black.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.r.d: It assumed the removed ball was white. If its color is unknown, the black case is possible too.
y-m-65-04.s.s1.explain: If the first ball is white (6/10), the chance the second is white is 5/9; if it is black (4/10), it is 6/9. (6/10)(5/9)+(4/10)(6/9)=54/90=6/10.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.prompt: You find out say ball wey dem put aside white. Now wetin be probability say second ball white?
y-m-65-04.s.s2.hint.0: Count the balls left in the bag again, separately for white and black.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with the earlier 6/10 and say whether it is the same or different, giving a reason.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.r.a: There are 9 balls left, but the number of white balls did not decrease.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.r.b: It thought the probability does not change even when you learn the information.
y-m-65-04.s.s2.r.c: This is because the remaining balls are 5 white and 4 black.
